opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing first, because I don't think any single report about export-control workarounds should drive a research agenda. If my approach swung every time a headline about lithography came out, that would mean it was resting on assumptions that were too fragile.

That said, it does sharpen something I've believed for a while. A lot of AI governance thinking has quietly leaned on compute as the chokepoint: if a handful of firms make the advanced chips, and those chips depend on EUV machines from basically one company, then you have a natural lever for monitoring and slowing things down. I've always seen that lever as real but temporary. Bottlenecks erode. Whether it takes three years or ten, you should assume that at some point frontier-scale compute will be available to more actors than you'd like, with less visibility than you'd like.

So what it reinforces for me is the case for safety approaches that don't depend on controlling who has the hardware. The core idea of guaranteed safe AI is that you don't just trust a powerful system because it behaved well in testing. You pair it with an explicit world model, a formal specification of what's acceptable, and a verifier that checks proposed actions or outputs against that specification before they touch anything important. The guarantee comes from the structure of the system, not from scarcity. Supply chains don't change that logic.

Where it does change my thinking is urgency and priorities. If the compute moat is shallower than people hoped, the window for building this infrastructure, meaning the modeling languages, the verification tooling, and the institutions that can say "this deployment comes with a proof of these properties," gets shorter. It also pushes me toward things that are easy to adopt, because the safety tooling has to be attractive to people who aren't regulated into using it. If a verified-safe workflow is also more reliable and more insurable, people will want it on its own merits.

The other piece is international. If capabilities are going to diffuse regardless, then a verifiable standard of safety is arguably more useful than a purely national one. You want something two parties who don't trust each other can both check, a bit like arms control verification. Mathematical guarantees have the nice property that you don't need to trust whoever produced them; you can check the proof yourself. That's a more robust foundation for cooperation than "we'll keep the machines away from you."

So I'd sum it up this way: it hasn't changed the destination, but it's made me more impatient about getting there, and more focused on making the safe path the one people would choose anyway.

r001.rationale: The response favors verifiable international safety standards, but does not say the original strategy depended on every actor with dangerous amounts of compute adopting a method through international coordination.

r002.rationale: It says compute bottlenecks erode and capability diffusion makes safety work more urgent, but does not argue that China’s effort undermines a coordinated AI slowdown regardless of whether it succeeds.

r003.rationale: The response calls for building safety infrastructure and making verified workflows attractive, but does not frame the revised objective as harnessing rapid AI development to build resilience against catastrophic risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it hasn't changed the core of my approach, but it has sharpened my sense of the timelines and the geopolitics around it, which matter a lot for how I think about adoption.

Let me separate those two things. The technical program for guaranteed safe AI is about building a different kind of pipeline. You have a world model that's written down explicitly, a safety specification that's written down explicitly, and a verifier that produces a proof, or at least a quantitative bound, that the AI system's outputs satisfy the specification relative to the world model. None of that depends on who controls EUV lithography. The math doesn't care whether the chips were fabbed in Taiwan or in Shanghai.

Where it does matter is in the strategic picture. A lot of the implicit theory of change in the West over the last few years has been something like: compute is the chokepoint, we can see the chokepoint, and that gives us a lever. Export controls buy time, and time is what you need if you want to get safety techniques mature before the most capable systems are deployed. If China genuinely routes around ASML, whether through domestic EUV, through alternative patterning approaches, or just through brute-force scaling of older nodes, then that lever gets weaker. You should discount the amount of time you think you're buying.

And I think that cuts in favor of the approach I've been pushing, not against it. If you believe you have a reliable compute moat, you can tell yourself a story where you develop frontier capabilities, keep them in a small number of hands, and manage risk through institutional controls and evals. If the moat is leaky, that story gets much less comfortable, because you have multiple actors at the frontier who don't fully trust each other, and evals alone can't give you the kind of assurance that would let those actors coordinate. What you want in a multipolar world is something that produces verifiable artifacts. A proof certificate is the kind of thing you can hand to a rival and they can check it without trusting you. That's qualitatively different from "our red team didn't find anything."

So the way I'd put it is that the ASML news makes me more urgent about the deployment and institutional side. It's not enough to have a research agenda. We need to be thinking about what the standards look like, what the verification infrastructure looks like, and how you build something that a Chinese lab and an American lab could both plausibly adopt, because they both have a self-interest in not being destroyed by their own systems.

The other thing I'd say is that I try hard not to overreact to any single piece of hardware news. These reports have a tendency to be either overstated or understated depending on who's doing the reporting, and the actual yields and costs of a domestic EUV effort are the kind of thing that only becomes clear years later. I'd rather design a program that's robust to a range of outcomes than one that depends on a particular bet about the state of Chinese lithography in 2028. If anything, that's the most honest answer: it made me want the whole thing to be less contingent on who has what compute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses standards that Chinese and American labs could adopt, but it does not state that Dalrymple’s original strategy depended on international coordination securing adoption by every actor with potentially dangerous compute.

r002.rationale: It says a successful route around ASML would weaken export controls’ leverage and reduce the time they buy. It does not argue that the credibility of the effort undermines a coordinated AI slowdown regardless of whether it succeeds.

r003.rationale: The response emphasizes verifiable safety methods and deployment standards, but does not frame the revised objective as using rapid AI development to build resilience against catastrophic risks.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the report itself from the implications if it’s true. I don’t have enough information here to assess how much progress China has actually made. But the possibility of advanced compute becoming more widely available makes it less attractive to rely on a hardware bottleneck as your primary safety strategy.

The motivation for guaranteed safe AI is to develop safety methods that hold up even as capabilities advance. The central question is: can we specify what a system must not do, model the environment in which it acts, and produce a checkable argument that its actions respect those constraints?

Of course, that guarantee depends on the assumptions. A proof about an inadequate model doesn’t establish safety in the real world. So specifying the constraints and validating the model are essential parts of the problem.

I’d frame the reported effort as a reason for urgency, rather than a change in the technical direction. We want safety mechanisms that can accompany increasingly capable systems, even in a world where access to compute is harder to control.

r001.rationale: The response describes developing safety methods that hold up as capabilities advance, but does not say the original strategy depended on international coordination securing adoption by every actor with dangerous amounts of compute.

r002.rationale: It says wider access to advanced compute would make a hardware bottleneck less attractive as a safety strategy. It does not argue that China’s effort undermines the viability of a coordinated AI slowdown regardless of whether the effort succeeds.

r003.rationale: The response calls the report a reason for urgency and says safety mechanisms should accompany increasingly capable systems, but does not frame the revised objective as harnessing rapid AI development to build resilience against catastrophic risks.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the specific report from the broader strategic question. I can’t assess from that report alone how much the hardware picture has changed. But if advanced compute becomes more widely available, that makes it more urgent to develop safety methods that don’t depend on controlling access to a particular supply chain.

The motivation for guaranteed safe AI is to make explicit what a system is allowed to do, what assumptions we’re making about its environment, and what evidence establishes that its behavior stays within those constraints. The guarantee is conditional on those assumptions, so getting them right is a substantial part of the work.

A development like this would affect the urgency and deployment strategy more than the technical foundation. You want safety mechanisms that are practical enough for people to adopt across different hardware platforms, even under competitive pressure. Ideally, we move toward a world where greater access to compute doesn’t automatically mean greater exposure to uncontrolled AI behavior.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety methods that can work across hardware platforms, but does not say the original strategy depended on international coordination or adoption by every actor with dangerous levels of compute.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the report alone does not establish how the hardware picture has changed. It does not argue that the prospect of China overcoming the bottleneck undermines a coordinated AI slowdown.

r003.rationale: The response calls for practical safety mechanisms as compute access expands, but does not frame the revised objective as using rapid AI development to build resilience against catastrophic risks.
